prize_parts.citation: for establishing biomolecular phase separation as a physical-chemical principle that organizes the living cell

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: biomolecular phase separation (B039) for Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen. The round-1 exchange did not dispute the central point, only its maturity. The concept is that cells organise chemistry through condensates governed by multivalency, saturation concentrations and phase behaviour, so that a membrane-free compartment is a thermodynamic outcome and not a structure that has to be built. Brangwynne and Hyman showed liquid behaviour of P granules in the living C. elegans embryo in 2009, Rosen's work showed how valency and affinity of interacting modules set the phase boundary quantitatively, and that framework has since been tested by many independent laboratories in vitro and, increasingly, with engineered and endogenous systems in cells. The principle is a new way of thinking about molecular organisation, is general across biology, and connects directly to neurodegeneration and amyloid, where it changes how aggregation is understood. It is also a physical-chemical result that a chemistry prize can credit as chemistry. The three names follow the origin of the liquid-state picture and the quantitative multivalency framework, which is the part of the field that is mature.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously after round 1 is maturity, and five colleagues have now put it to me (Aqvist, Brzezinski, Chabes, Linke and, in effect, Aili's comparison with degraders). It remains contested which endogenous condensates are equilibrium phases rather than other assemblies, in-cell measurements at native concentrations are thinner than in vitro droplet work, and the physiological function of many condensates is not settled. A citation phrased around a principle can be accused of running ahead of the evidence in cells. Attribution is also compromised by the three-person cap, which leaves out Pappu and Mittag (sequence-encoded phase behaviour of disordered regions) and others. Finally, my configuration has a single explicit supporter and will probably not reach five votes, whereas B044 has four explicit supporters. I do not treat that count as an argument, but it is a real constraint on what the committee can decide.

responses.point: Linke asked which testable prediction of the phase-separation framework has been confirmed in living cells and not only in vitro, and said that an answer would change his view.
responses.response: The clearest in vivo tests I can point to are those that follow from the physics: a liquid should fuse, drip and relax its shape under surface tension, and a phase should have a threshold concentration above which it forms and below which it does not. P granules in the embryo show the first behaviours, and the threshold behaviour has been tested by driving the concentration of a protein in living cells across a boundary, for example with light-induced oligomerisation, and finding that condensates form above a saturation concentration that depends on valency in the way the in vitro phase diagram says. That is a prediction confirmed in cells. I will not overstate it, because these are mostly engineered or overexpressed systems and the same quantitative test on endogenous condensates is the gap you are pointing at. So my answer is that the principle is tested in vivo, the generality is not, and I would ask you to weigh that as I do, as incomplete scope and not a failure of the central idea.

responses.point: Chabes accepts that the concept is important but wants quantitative evidence that in-cell condensates are equilibrium phases at native concentrations, and calls this the youngest field on the shortlist.
responses.response: I accept the criticism and your standard for what counts as measured. I would note that the same objection runs through your own preferred B044 in a different form, since the argument there rests on mechanism and on independent reproduction and not on an approved drug. What I would add is that the committee does not have to certify every cellular body as a phase to credit the principle. The credit is for showing that multivalency and phase thermodynamics are a route to cellular organisation, which is demonstrated. Where I concede your point is timing: you are right that a skeptical majority is rational here, and I do not think five votes can be reached on interpretations that are still being measured. I have kept my position because I believe it is the strongest scientific case I see, not because I expect it to win.

responses.point: Aqvist ranked B039 last because he is not convinced it is chemistry in the sense of a quantitative, settled mechanism, and wants the in-cell debate to settle before supporting it over degraders.
responses.response: I think that is the fairest statement of the disagreement. My view is that the quantitative content is not absent: saturation concentrations, tie lines, the dependence of phase boundaries on valency and affinity, and Flory-Huggins-type descriptions are used to fit and predict data, which is physical chemistry in the ordinary sense. What I cannot offer is a settled picture of every in-cell case. I also take your point that degraders have demonstrated consequences while condensates are still partly a framework. Where we differ is on whether consequences must be clinical. A concept that changed what questions chemists and biologists ask is also a consequence, and I would weigh it so.

responses.point: Aili finds degraders the most persuasive broadly supported candidate, sees B051 as the strongest alternative if maturity is preferred over novelty, and does not see a configuration cleaner than the B039 trio.
responses.response: Thank you for the attribution point on B051: dropping Anderson from a Cullis, Hope and Madden trio was a mistake on my part, and I now think any lipid nanoparticle configuration needs Cullis and Anderson at least, which tells me B051 would also face a hard three-name choice. Your statement that you do not see degraders as a weaker candidate than B039 is reasonable, and after this round I find the Crews, Deshaies and Handa trio coherent: Handa's cereblon work is the identification step that explains the glue half, which Linke and Aqvist also accept. My difference with you is that I still put the more general concept first. If the committee finds B039 premature, B044 is where my vote would go and I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Brzezinski prefers nitrogenase for Rees, Einsle and Seefeldt on structural confirmation over three decades, and ranks B039 last, wanting an expert view on whether it is chemistry or physiology.
responses.response: On chemistry versus physiology, I would say that the phase behaviour of multivalent macromolecules, with its thermodynamics and its dependence on interaction strength, is chemistry, and the physiological readout is what makes it consequential. I agree the nitrogenase structural chain is the more mature and cleanly attributed, and I take your point that your candidate is less visible because of its indirect impact. My caution about B032 is the one you share, that the catalytic cycle is only partly resolved, so a citation of structure and mechanism would claim more than the field has settled. A citation limited to the cofactor structure would be safe, but then the comparison with B039 would be about maturity versus breadth of concept, and that is a judgment I would make differently.

uncertainties: Whether the in-cell evidence for equilibrium phase behaviour of endogenous condensates is strong enough this year; I accept the committee may judge it is not.
Whether Rosen or Pappu and Mittag should hold the third place; I keep Rosen for the quantitative multivalency framework but the choice is not clean.
Whether my position can reach five votes given only one explicit supporter, in which case my vote would be a first-choice statement and my fallback would be B044 for Crews, Deshaies and Handa.
Whether a citation tied to a principle rather than to a drug or a structure can be worded so that it does not overstate cellular generality.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal. I share Lund University with Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, and my research on lipid self-assembly and amyloid is scientifically close to B039 and B051, but I have no personal or institutional tie to any credited person on the shortlist.
